title: Master by Research in the UK: Fees and Entry (2027)
excerpt: Thinking about a Master by Research in the UK? Here are the typical fees, entry requirements, visa rules and whether you can bring dependants for 2027 entry.

What Is a Master by Research (MRes)?

A Master by Research (MRes) is a one-year postgraduate degree in which most of your time goes on an independent research project instead of lectures. You usually take a small number of training modules in research methods, then complete a dissertation or thesis under a supervisor.

It suits students who want to move toward a PhD, work in R&D or policy, or build a deeper specialism than a taught Master's allows. A taught MSc, by contrast, is built around classes, exams and a shorter dissertation.

MRes vs. Taught Master's: Which Should You Choose?

MResTaught MSc/MA
Main focusResearch projectClasses + dissertation
AssessmentThesis, research portfolioExams, coursework, dissertation
Best forPhD path, research careersIndustry roles, career change
SupervisorClose, one-to-oneModule leaders, one dissertation supervisor
Dependants (visa)Possible (research-based course)Generally not allowed

If your goal is a job in industry within a year, a taught Master's is usually the more direct route. If you want to test whether a PhD is right for you, MRes is a lower-risk first step.

Fees and Entry Requirements for 2027

Tuition for international students varies widely by university and subject. Lab-based subjects such as engineering and biosciences cost more than humanities. As a rough guide, expect about £14,000 to £25,000 for the year. These are approximate figures, so always confirm the fee for your exact course.

  • Academic: a good Bachelor's degree, usually equivalent to a UK 2:1, in a relevant subject.
  • English: typically IELTS 6.5 overall, with no less than 5.5–6.0 in each skill. Some universities accept PTE or Duolingo.
  • Research proposal: many MRes courses ask for a short proposal or a named supervisor.
  • References: academic referees who can speak to your research potential.
💡
Choose the supervisor firstA clear, realistic research idea and a supervisor whose work matches it can matter more than your grades alone.

Can You Bring Dependants on an MRes?

Since January 2024, most international Master's students can no longer bring dependants. The exception is research-based postgraduate courses. Universities treat MRes degrees as research-based, so students on a full-time MRes of nine months or longer may be able to bring a partner and children.

⚠️
Check your CASFor a research-based course, your CAS should show it is research-based. Ask the university to confirm this in writing before you plan to bring family. Dependants also have to meet their own funds and visa requirements.

Visa Funds and Work After Your MRes

For a Student visa you must show maintenance funds for up to nine months: £1,171/£1,529 per month now, rising to £1,203/£1,570 from 30 November 2026. For nine months that is about £10,827 outside London or £14,130 in London after the increase, on top of your first-year tuition balance. The Student visa fee is £558 and the Immigration Health Surcharge is £776 per year.

After your degree, the Graduate Route lets you stay and work for a set period. For applications from 1 January 2027, that period is 18 months. A research degree can also open the way to a PhD or a Skilled Worker role.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is an MRes the same as an MPhil?
No. An MRes is a one-year Master's with training modules and a research project. An MPhil is usually a longer, fully research-based degree.
Is MRes funded?
Most international MRes students are self-funded, though some universities offer partial scholarships. Check each university's scholarship page.
Will an MRes help me get a PhD?
Often yes. It shows you can complete independent research, and many universities treat it as strong preparation for doctoral study.
